opus-5.5.text:
For me, writing code was never just a job. It's how I think. Ever since I was a kid, programming has been the way I figure out whether I really understand something. If I can implement it and it runs and the result looks right, then I understand it. If I can't, I'm probably fooling myself.

When you start a company, the natural path is that you write less and less code. You're hiring, fundraising, talking to customers, setting direction, dealing with all the organizational stuff. Those things matter, and I take them seriously. But I've watched a lot of technical founders slowly drift away from the technology, and after a few years they can't really judge whether a technical decision is good. They depend entirely on other people's opinions, and you can feel the company losing its technical taste.

So my worry has a few layers. First, I'd lose touch with the details, and with something like Taichi, or graphics and compilers in general, the details are everything. A small design choice in the IR or the memory layout can decide whether a system is ten times faster or ten times slower. If I'm not close to the code, I can't sense those things anymore.

Second, there's the joy. Coding is one of the few activities where I get into a really deep flow state. If I spend every day in meetings, I'm afraid I'll become someone who's very busy but not very happy, and eventually that affects how well I lead.

Third, there's credibility with the team. Engineers respect people who can still roll up their sleeves. If I can sit down, read a PR, find the bug, or prototype an idea over a weekend, the conversation is completely different from just saying "I think we should do X."

So I try to protect some time to keep writing code, even if it's not on the critical path. It keeps my mind sharp and keeps me honest about what's actually hard. I don't want to become a founder who only talks about technology.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a founder who drifts from the technology loses the ability to judge technical choices, and that staying close to code keeps them honest about what is actually hard.

r002.rationale: The candidate lists noncoding founder duties but does not distinguish being hands-on from personally writing code.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses judging technical decisions but does not connect understanding technology to making business decisions.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I did worry about it, quite a lot in the early days of Taichi, because writing code was my identity. I spent my whole PhD at MIT building Taichi, line by line, and the compiler, the language, the autodiff system — those were things I personally understood down to the last detail. When you become a founder, you gradually hand that over. First you stop writing the hard parts, then you stop reviewing every pull request, and one day you realize there are entire modules you've never opened.

The fear is really two things. One is losing taste. A technical founder's biggest asset is being able to tell what's good engineering and what's not, and I was afraid that if I stopped coding, that intuition would decay. The other is losing credibility with the team. Engineers can tell very quickly whether a leader actually understands the problem or is just repeating things they heard in meetings.

What I eventually realized is that the thing I cared about was never the typing. It was the ability to make a system work, to go from a vague idea to something real. As a founder, the system you're building is just bigger — it includes people, customers, the product roadmap, the company itself. And you can still keep your hands dirty in a smaller way. I still read code, I still prototype when something interests me, and that keeps the intuition alive. But if I insisted on writing most of the code myself, I'd be the bottleneck, and the project would be limited by one person's output. Letting go turned out to be the only way to let it grow beyond me.

r001.rationale: The candidate says founders may stop reviewing code and encounter modules they have never opened, risking decay in engineering intuition and understanding of the team's problems.

r002.rationale: The candidate separates building a larger system as a founder from personally writing most of its code, while describing reading code and prototyping as ways to stay hands-on.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses engineering judgment, team credibility, and broader company-building, but does not state that understanding how technology works helps leaders make business decisions.

astra-6.text:
I think the worry is that, as a founder, you can become disconnected from what you’re actually building. When you write code, you get very direct feedback: this works, this doesn’t, this is harder than we thought. If you only sit in meetings, it’s easy to lose that intuition.

Of course, you also have to recognize that writing code isn’t always the most valuable use of your time. Sometimes the team needs you to hire someone or talk to a customer. So for me, it’s about staying close enough to the technical work to make good decisions, while giving other people room to build.

r001.rationale: It says a founder who stops coding can become disconnected from what they are building and lose direct feedback and intuition.

r002.rationale: It says coding is not always the best use of the founder’s time, while they can stay close to technical work and let others build.

r003.rationale: It connects staying close to technical work with retaining intuition and making good decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the worry is that if I stop writing code, I lose touch with what we’re actually building. As a founder, you hear about problems through meetings and reports, but when you write code yourself, you feel the friction directly. You understand which things are easy, which things are hard, and where the tools need to improve.

And I enjoy it. That’s a big part of why I started doing this. Of course, that doesn’t mean I should write every line of code. The company needs me to do other things too. But I’d like to stay hands-on enough that my technical judgment comes from actually building things.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that stopping coding risks losing touch with what the company is building and the friction involved in doing it.

r002.rationale: It says the founder need not write every line and should stay hands-on, but does not explain how a founder can remain hands-on without personally writing code.

r003.rationale: It connects building things to technical judgment, but does not state that understanding technology helps leaders make business decisions.
